messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Javier has spent his entire career creating safe spaces for others. As a social ministry worker, he counsels the homeless, connects families with resources, and offers a calm presence in the midst of chaos. For the last six months, however, his own world has felt anything but safe. The finalization of his divorce from his partner, Marco, was supposed to be a relief, but it has only solidified a profound sense of isolation and fear that began on one specific night. That evening, an argument had escalated in a way it never had before. The sharp smell of whiskey on Marco’s breath filled their small apartment as his voice grew louder, culminating in the deafening slam of their bedroom door. Javier remembers being pushed to the floor, the rough texture of the rug against his cheek, and the terrifying weight of Marco holding him down, his arms pinned, unable to move or even breathe properly.

The memory of that night is not a distant story he tells himself; it is a landscape he is forced to revisit. It returns with a startling clarity, the images so vivid he can almost feel the pressure on his chest again. Sometimes, it is the sounds that ambush him—Marco's slurred, angry words echoing in his head as if he were right there in the room. When these memories surface, they bring with them a wave of overwhelming grief, not for the lost love, but for the loss of his own belief in his safety and judgment. The vividness of these recollections has made the world feel treacherous, sensitizing him to any reminder of that night. A memory of being restrained can make a friendly hand on his shoulder feel like an imminent attack, turning a simple gesture into a potent trigger.

His life is now governed by a constant, humming sense of threat. He startles violently at any unexpected movement in his periphery, a flinch he tries to hide from his colleagues at the community center. Night is the worst; the darkness seems to amplify every sound, and he finds it impossible to feel secure. This pervasive feeling of danger has driven him to adopt a series of rigid, exhausting routines. He checks the locks on his new apartment’s doors and windows repeatedly before bed, a ritual that offers only fleeting reassurance. The constant state of vigilance seems to keep the trauma fresh in his mind, ensuring the memories remain sharp and easily accessible, as if his brain is refusing to let its guard down. It has also made him acutely attuned to his triggers, turning his environment into a minefield of potential threats.

These triggers now dictate the boundaries of his shrinking world. The sound of a door slamming shut—a common occurrence at the busy ministry—instantly sends a jolt of panic through him, making him feel trapped and endangered. That sudden noise often brings back a fragment of the memory, the sound of his own bedroom door closing off his escape. In response to these moments, he has learned to freeze completely, a deer-in-headlights stillness that can last for several seconds. He also meticulously avoids the entire neighborhood where he and Marco used to live, even though it means cutting himself off from friends and familiar places. He had hoped that this avoidance, along with his fierce attempts to control and suppress any show of emotion, would keep the memories at bay. Instead, these strategies seem to have backfired; by treating the memories as threats to be contained, they have only gained power, ambushing him with greater intensity when his guard is down. His efforts to maintain a calm exterior only seem to make him more susceptible to being triggered by a sudden sound or the smell of alcohol on a client’s breath.

The cycle has become self-sustaining. A trigger, like the smell of alcohol during a counseling session, activates his sense of immediate threat and brings the memory rushing back. His feeling of being in danger compels him to retreat, to lock his doors, to avoid. This avoidance, in turn, makes the outside world seem even more menacing and his triggers more powerful. He came to therapy last week after an incident at work. A man he was counseling, distraught and smelling of beer, had reached out and grabbed his arm to steady himself. Javier froze, his breath catching in his throat, unable to speak or move. The man, confused and concerned by his reaction, had backed away. In that moment, Javier realized his own trauma was now a barrier to the work that once gave his life meaning. He is terrified that he is permanently broken, but he holds onto the hope that he might one day feel safe enough in his own skin to help others feel safe in theirs.
